design_detail: Double-blind, placebo-controlled, within-person laboratory brain-imaging study in 9 healthy volunteers (7 men, 2 women) who had used ecstasy before, at the University of Chicago: three sessions at least 6 days apart (on average 10.7 days, SD 7.2) with MDMA 0.75 mg/kg and 1.5 mg/kg given in ascending order and placebo placed at random among the sessions; sessions began at noon and volunteers stayed in hospital at least 4.5 hours. About 85 minutes after the capsule they lay in a 3-tesla scanner and viewed angry, fearful, happy and neutral faces (and a motor-visual control task). Measures: Drug Effects Questionnaire (DEQ; the 'feel drug' item reported), a 7-item visual analogue scale (VAS; the 'sociable' item reported), the Profile of Mood States (POMS; the Friendliness scale reported), blood pressure and heart rate, and brain response in a priori regions (amygdala, ventral striatum). Peak changes and repeated-measures analyses of variance with paired t tests; alpha .05 for the analyses and .01 for post hoc tests; brain tests at voxel p < .005 uncorrected, with small-volume correction in the a priori regions.
can_establish: Whether, in 9 healthy volunteers with earlier ecstasy use, a single oral dose of MDMA raised peak 'feel drug' ratings, systolic pressure and heart rate above placebo (F(2,16) 98.6, 41.9 and 21.9), with 'feel drug' and systolic pressure also higher at the higher dose; whether 1.5 mg/kg raised the 'sociable' rating from baseline at 135 minutes more than 0.75 mg/kg did (p < .01); and, as an early report, that left amygdala response to angry faces was lower at 1.5 mg/kg and ventral striatum response to happy faces higher at 0.75 mg/kg than on placebo.
cannot_establish: That MDMA raises sociability against placebo (the difference from placebo was p = .04, which the paper's own post hoc cut-off of .01 and its text call marginal); that sociability rises with dose (dose and session order are mixed up, since doses were given in ascending order); that the brain changes cause feeling more sociable (no link is tested); that the amygdala result is firm (corrected p = .052); that the brain results are not a general effect of MDMA on blood flow (activity also fell in visual and motor cortex); anything about people new to MDMA (all had used it, 2 to 300 times); unwanted effects beyond one sentence (the anxious, sedated, down and nauseated ratings were collected but not reported); plasma levels (not measured).

sample.recruitment: Online advertisements and word of mouth (Materials and Methods > Participants).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Healthy, right-handed volunteers aged 18 to 29 who reported ecstasy use at least twice. Excluded: lifetime psychotic or bipolar disorder; past-year other Axis I disorder; medical or neurological illness (medical examination, electrocardiogram and clinical interview); body mass index outside 18 to 30; an earlier adverse response to ecstasy; any reason not to be scanned (Materials and Methods > Participants).
sample.demographics: Mean age 24.0 (SD 3.2); two of nine women; six identified as Caucasian. Lifetime ecstasy use 2 to 300 occasions (mean 63.9, SD 94.9), first use at about 17.4 years, last use 0.5 to 24 months before the study (mean 10.2); four had used ecstasy in the past year. In the past month five smoked daily (about 10 cigarettes a day), five used cannabis at least once and eight drank alcohol; all nine had used cannabis, eight stimulants and seven hallucinogens in their lifetime (Results > 1st paragraph; Table 1).
sample.attrition: None reported for the self-report data; three emotion-recognition runs and three motor-visual runs were excluded from the imaging data for head movement (Materials and Methods > Imaging).
sample.selection_effects: Nine volunteers with earlier ecstasy use, recruited by advertisement, screened for health and for any earlier bad response; the authors say all had prior exposure for ethical reasons and that exposure varied widely. A sample this small and this heterogeneous cannot show how most people respond.

exposure.measurement: Opaque size 00 gelatin capsules with MDMA and lactose, or lactose placebo; no plasma concentrations were measured, which the authors name as a limitation. The source of the MDMA is not stated in the text read.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: a single oral dose of 0.75 mg/kg or 1.5 mg/kg (ascending order) or placebo, one per session, at least 6 days apart; no food for 2 hours before each session.
exposure.polysubstance: Abstinence required from cannabis for 7 days, alcohol for 24 hours and other recreational drugs for 48 hours before sessions, checked by urine, saliva and breath tests; five volunteers smoked cigarettes daily.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Cannabis 7 days, alcohol 24 hours, other recreational drugs 48 hours; verified by urine test (Rapid Check 9 Panel), saliva test (Oratect III) and breathalyser; a pregnancy test for women at each session.

comparison.controls: Placebo and both doses in the same people (double-blind); placebo placed at random among the three sessions, the two doses in ascending order.
comparison.matching: Within person. The authors say session order had no effect on the subjective, cardiovascular or brain results, citing the partial randomisation and the interval between sessions; no statistics are printed.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Plasma MDMA not measured; earlier ecstasy use varied from 2 to 300 occasions and the authors checked it against brain signal by correlation (none found).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Abstinence rules and tests; current cannabis, alcohol and tobacco use was allowed outside those windows and is reported.

outcomes.instruments: Drug Effects Questionnaire (four visual analogue items: feel any drug effect, like the drug effect, feel high, want more; 'feel drug' reported); a 7-item visual analogue scale (stimulated, anxious, sedated, down, elated, sociable, nauseated; 'sociable' reported); Profile of Mood States (72 adjectives, 8 subscales; Friendliness reported); blood pressure and heart rate; functional magnetic resonance imaging during an emotion-recognition task and a motor-visual task. DEQ and VAS at 0, 30, 60, 135, 210 and 240 minutes after the capsule; POMS at 0, 60 and 240 minutes (Materials and Methods > Protocol, 3rd paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: Established scales cited (Johanson and Uhlenhuth 1980; Folstein and Luria 1973; McNair and Droppleman 1971); the choice of 'sociable' and 'Friendliness' as the subjective outcomes was made on the basis of the hypotheses stated in the Introduction.
outcomes.operationalization: Peak change from before the capsule for blood pressure, heart rate and 'feel drug'; change from baseline over time for 'sociable' and Friendliness, with drug-by-time interaction and then the 135-minute point. Brain: a priori regions as 10 mm spheres (amygdala; ventral striatum).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Editors' count of 11 rows in Table 2 (3 cardiovascular, 1 'feel drug', 2 sociability, 1 friendliness, 4 emotion recognition), plus the imaging tests: whole-brain voxel tests at p < .005 uncorrected in a priori regions, followed by small-volume correction, and p < .001 uncorrected for exploratory whole-brain maps. Post hoc subjective tests used alpha .01.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double blind; no check of the blind is reported. A 1.5 mg/kg dose with a 'feel drug' rating averaging 92 of 100 is unlikely to have been concealed.

analysis.effect_sizes: Table 2, mean (SD as printed) for placebo, 0.75 and 1.5 mg/kg. Peak change from before the capsule: systolic pressure 4.8 (19.0), 34.8 (13.5), 48.1 (11.6) mm Hg, F(2,16) 41.9; diastolic 3.6 (13.9), 15.8 (13.4), 26.0 (5.1), F 8.0; heart rate -5.3 (11.0), 19.7 (16.2), 35.3 (19.9), F 21.9; DEQ 'feel drug' 14.5 (5.0), 57.1 (4.6), 91.8 (4.0), F 98.6 (all p < .05); the SDs for 'feel drug' look like standard errors (editors' calculation: t(8) = 16.1 for 1.5 mg/kg against placebo implies an SD of the difference of about 14). VAS 'sociable' change at 135 minutes -6.3 (17.7), -9.5 (13.5), 19.7 (24.7), F(2,16) 7.3; placebo against 1.5 mg/kg t(8) = 2.5, p = .04 (called marginal; post hoc alpha .01); 0.75 against 1.5 mg/kg t(8) = 3.8, p < .01; drug-by-time F(8,64) 3.1, partial eta-squared .28. POMS Friendliness F(2,16) 1.3, not significant. Emotion recognition accuracy .89, .91, .86 (F 0.9) and reaction time (F 3.1) not significantly changed. Imaging: left amygdala to angry against neutral faces F(2,16) 9.64, p < .005; placebo greater than 1.5 mg/kg t(8) 4.41, p < .005; small-volume corrected p = .052; no effect for fearful faces; ventral striatum to happy against neutral faces F(2,16) 9.75, p < .005; 0.75 mg/kg greater than placebo t(8) 6.13, p < .001, corrected p < .05; 1.5 mg/kg against placebo t(8) 2.72, not surviving correction.
analysis.covariates: None (within person); lifetime ecstasy use and time since last use were correlated with extracted brain signal (no correlations).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration is mentioned; three directional hypotheses (self-rated sociability up; amygdala response to threat down; ventral striatum response to happy faces up) are stated at the end of the Introduction.
analysis.selective_reporting: Four DEQ items, 7 VAS items and 8 POMS subscales were collected but the paper reports three subjective measures; anxious, sedated, down, nauseated, 'like the drug effect', 'feel high' and 'want more' are not reported, nor are the other POMS subscales. The abstract says 1.5 mg/kg increased sociability against placebo as well as against 0.75 mg/kg, and that MDMA attenuated amygdala response to angry faces; the text calls the placebo difference marginal (p = .04 against a post hoc alpha of .01), and the amygdala result is p = .052 after correction.
analysis.power: No power calculation. Nine volunteers; the authors say the sample was small and the findings need replication in a larger sample. They suggest the non-significant Friendliness effect may reflect sample size, citing a large effect size for the main effect of drug (partial eta-squared above .23); that statistic is not printed, and the printed drug-by-time F(2,16) 1.3 gives a partial eta-squared of 0.14 (editors' calculation).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 9 volunteers with earlier ecstasy use, MDMA raised 'feel drug' ratings in a dose-related way (peak change 14.5 on placebo, 57.1 at 0.75 mg/kg, 91.8 at 1.5 mg/kg) and raised blood pressure and heart rate; no serious adverse effects were seen. The 'sociable' rating at 135 minutes changed by -6.3 on placebo, -9.5 at 0.75 mg/kg and +19.7 at 1.5 mg/kg; the 1.5 mg/kg rating was above 0.75 mg/kg (p < .01) and, by the paper's own account, only marginally above placebo (p = .04); the POMS Friendliness scale did not change significantly. Left amygdala response to angry faces was lower at 1.5 mg/kg than on placebo (uncorrected p < .005, corrected p = .052) and ventral striatum response to happy faces higher at 0.75 mg/kg (corrected p < .05); activity in visual and motor cortex also fell. Accuracy and speed of recognising faces did not change.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says MDMA at 1.5 mg/kg increased self-reported sociability compared with placebo and with 0.75 mg/kg, that it attenuated left amygdala response to angry faces, and that the data are the first evidence that MDMA may increase sociability by diminishing responses to threat and enhancing responses to reward; the Discussion says the findings are preliminary and need replication.

timeline.event: Hysek et al. (Basel, 32 volunteers): MDMA 125 mg raised ratings of feeling happy, open and close to others against placebo, and lowered recognition of several negative faces; they cite this study for the lower amygdala response to threat.

Kirkpatrick et al. (pooled Chicago, San Francisco and Basel, 220 volunteers): similar peak ratings of drug effect and drug liking at three sites; closeness to others higher at San Francisco than at Basel.

replication.where_it_stands: Raised self-rated feelings of closeness and good mood after MDMA are reported by other laboratories; the brain-imaging results (amygdala, ventral striatum) were not tested again in the papers read here. The sociability rating against placebo is a marginal result in this study.

funding.affiliations_note: The senior author is also the senior author of the Chicago studies pooled by Kirkpatrick et al. (2014); whether these nine volunteers are among those 95 is not stated.

what_would_settle_it: A larger preregistered study with randomised dose order (or different people at each dose), plasma MDMA at the time of imaging, a control region and a cerebral blood flow measure analysed in the same model, correction across brain regions, a placebo comparison for sociability that meets its own threshold, and behaviour toward other people rather than ratings.

domains.note: Placebo placed at random; MDMA doses given in ascending order for safety; how the placement was generated is not described.
At least 6 days between sessions (average 10.7, SD 7.2); the authors say a longer gap may have been needed to exclude carry-over, and report no order effect without statistics.
Double blind, but the dose-related effect at 1.5 mg/kg is obvious; no check of the blind.
All 9 are described; three emotion-recognition and three motor-visual imaging runs were excluded for movement without saying whose.

Self-ratings by people who could feel the drug; brain signal may reflect blood-flow effects of MDMA (activity in visual and motor cortex also fell); plasma MDMA not measured; printed SDs for 'feel drug' look like standard errors.

Three of the collected subjective measures reported; the abstract's sociability result against placebo does not meet the paper's own post hoc threshold (p = .04 against .01); the headline amygdala result is p = .052 after correction; no registration.

domains.domain: Dose comparison, 0.75 against 1.5 mg/kg (added by the editors; not a RoB 2 domain)
domains.note: Ascending order mixes up dose and order; nine volunteers; the dose-dependence of sociability rests on this contrast.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The large dose-related changes in 'feel drug' ratings, blood pressure and heart rate in the same people are at some concerns at worst. The overall judgment is set by the selective reporting of the sociability and brain results and by the ascending dose order. The source may be cited for the design, the sample, the dose-related feel-drug ratings and cardiovascular changes, and as a small early report of a rise in a 'sociable' rating at 1.5 mg/kg that was marginal against placebo; it should not be cited as showing that MDMA raises sociability against placebo, a dose-response for sociability, or the brain findings as established.

key_findings.finding: Design: 9 healthy, right-handed volunteers aged 18 to 29 with earlier ecstasy use (at least twice), recruited by advertisement and word of mouth; a three-session within-person double-blind design with MDMA 0.75 mg/kg and 1.5 mg/kg in ascending order and placebo placed at random, at least 6 days apart, sessions at noon, at least 4.5 hours in hospital; abstinence from cannabis for 7 days, alcohol 24 hours and other drugs 48 hours, checked by urine, saliva and breath tests.
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods > Participants, 1st paragraph; Protocol, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Sample: 7 men and 2 women, mean age 24.0 (SD 3.2); lifetime ecstasy use 2 to 300 occasions (mean 63.9, SD 94.9), 4 of 9 in the past year; all had used cannabis, 8 stimulants and 7 hallucinogens; in the past month 5 smoked daily.

Peak 'feel drug' rating (change from before the capsule, DEQ) 14.5 on placebo, 57.1 at 0.75 mg/kg and 91.8 at 1.5 mg/kg (F(2,16) 98.6); peak systolic pressure rose 4.8, 34.8 and 48.1 mm Hg and heart rate -5.3, 19.7 and 35.3 beats a minute; there were no serious adverse effects.
key_findings.note: The printed SDs for 'feel drug' (5.0, 4.6, 4.0) look like standard errors.

key_findings.finding: 'Sociable' rating (VAS), change from baseline at 135 minutes: -6.3 on placebo, -9.5 at 0.75 mg/kg and +19.7 at 1.5 mg/kg; drug-by-time F(8,64) 3.1 (partial eta-squared .28); 1.5 against 0.75 mg/kg t(8) 3.8, p < .01; 1.5 mg/kg against placebo t(8) 2.5, p = .04, described as marginal against the post hoc alpha of .01. POMS Friendliness showed a similar pattern that was not significant (F(2,16) 1.3).
key_findings.locator: Results > 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Table 2; Figure 2 legend

key_findings.finding: Imaging: left amygdala response to angry against neutral faces was lower at 1.5 mg/kg than on placebo (uncorrected p < .005; corrected p = .052) and not changed for fearful faces; ventral striatum response to happy against neutral faces was higher at 0.75 mg/kg than on placebo (corrected p < .05) and at 1.5 mg/kg did not survive correction; activity in visual and motor cortex fell at 1.5 mg/kg; accuracy and speed of recognising faces did not change.

Limits stated by the authors: findings preliminary and the sample small; only two a priori brain regions; possible blood-flow effects on the signal; all volunteers had earlier ecstasy exposure, varying widely; doses in ascending order for safety, 6 days minimum between sessions, no order effect found; no plasma MDMA measured.

The Introduction says increased sociability and decreased defensiveness are cited by people who use ecstasy as a motivator to use it (citing a survey, Sumnall et al. 2006) and that human laboratory studies of 1 to 2 mg/kg report increased extroversion, friendliness, sociability, talkativeness and closeness, with some studies not finding them; this paper's data do not address why people take MDMA.
key_findings.note: Second-hand statement; Sumnall et al. (2006) was not read.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says 1.5 mg/kg increased self-reported sociability compared with placebo. Table 2 gives placebo against 1.5 mg/kg as t(8) 2.5, p = .04, and the text and Figure 2 legend call it a marginal difference, against the paper's own post hoc alpha of .01.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's sociability result against placebo is not significant by the paper's own rule; only the contrast with 0.75 mg/kg (p < .01) is.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says 1.5 mg/kg attenuated left amygdala response to angry faces compared with placebo; after small-volume correction for the a priori region the result is p = .052.
reporting_issues.consequence: The headline imaging result does not meet the conventional threshold once corrected; the paper calls its findings preliminary.

reporting_issues.issue: For POMS Friendliness the text says the main effect of drug was large (partial eta-squared above .23), so a missing significance may reflect sample size; the main-effect statistic is not printed, and the printed drug-by-time F(2,16) 1.3 gives a partial eta-squared of 0.14 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The effect-size statement cannot be checked against Table 2; the Friendliness result is not significant by any printed test.

reporting_issues.issue: The 'feel drug' values in Table 2 are printed as standard deviations (5.0, 4.6, 4.0) but behave like standard errors: t(8) 16.1 for 1.5 mg/kg against placebo implies an SD of the paired difference of about 14 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The spread of 'feel drug' ratings between volunteers is larger than printed.

reporting_issues.issue: Anxious, sedated, down, nauseated, 'like the drug effect', 'feel high' and 'want more' were collected but are not reported, nor are seven of the eight POMS subscales; unwanted effects are covered by one sentence (no serious adverse effects).
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper cannot say how often unpleasant feelings occurred at either dose.

reporting_issues.issue: MDMA doses were given in ascending order, so dose is mixed up with session order; the authors report no order effect without statistics.
reporting_issues.consequence: A dose-response for sociability or for brain responses cannot be separated from order, practice or carry-over.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC3328967 (author manuscript), read in the app's browser: abstract, Introduction, Materials and Methods, Results, Tables 1 to 3, figure legends, Discussion, acknowledgments. Figures 1 to 4 are images and were not read for values.
